name: Sibutu Sama
catalog_quote: 5.2.2 Primary stress always occurs on the penultimate syllable of words having two or more syllables. || 5.2.3 Words having two and three syllables carry only primary stress. || 5.2.4 Words having only four syllables carry a single secondary stress on the first syllable.

new_statements.quote: Primary stress in PSB occurs regularly on the vowel of the penultimate syllable of the word, reconstructed on the basis of its reflex on the penult in all SB languages except in predictable environments in NB. This observation applies to words, not merely to stems, so that suffixation results in the shift of stress to the right. Example from CS.2: bónoq 'to kill'; amónoq 'kills'; bonóqun 'kill it'; pagbonóqbi 'your act of fighting together'; pagbonoqánbi 'the cause of your fighting together'. [p. 277:] Note that stress in all Sama-Bajaw languages falls on the penult, with rare exceptions which are indicated.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog (StressTyp2) records penultimate primary stress for Sibutu Sama (stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 10010 (1 = a stressed syllable), with an initial secondary beat in 4+ syllable words). Pallesen agrees on the penult primary and adds that the domain is the suffixed word (stress shifts right under suffixation), that stress is predictable/non-phonemic across Sama-Bajaw, and that the schwa-penult exception is confined to Sabah Land Bajaw. He says nothing about secondary stress, so the catalog's initial secondary is neither confirmed nor contradicted. The statement is made at the level of PSB/all SB languages rather than for Sama Sibutuq specifically, but SS.4 is…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the whole word (not the stem), so it moves rightward when suffixes are added; this is reconstructed for Proto-Sama-Bajaw and stated to hold in all Sama-Bajaw daughter languages, of which Sama Sibutuq (Pallesen's SS.4) is one of the six with completed phonemic analysis. Sec. 5.1.3 (p. 164) adds: 'Predictable word stress is a feature of all SB daughter languages including AB', i.e. stress is non-contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned anywhere in the work.
new_statements.exceptions: The only stated departure from penult stress is in NB (Sabah Land Bajaw), not in the Sulu Sama languages: 'In NB stress occurs on the penult except when the vowel of the penult is the mid central vowel /ə/, in which case it occurs on the ultima', with reduction of an inherited geminate (PSB *bə́lli 'to buy' > NB.1 bəlí) (p. 94). The appendix says penult stress holds in all Sama-Bajaw languages 'with rare exceptions which are indicated'; no exception is marked in the Sama Sibutuq entry (p. 282: Sinama, əlliŋ sibutuq, bahasa sibutuq).
new_statements.identity_note: Pallesen's stress statement is for Proto-Sama-Bajaw and 'all SB languages'; Sibutu Sama is his SS.4 'Sama Sibutuq' (Sibutu Island, 45 km SW of Bongao, and Sarvel Bay, Sabah; c. 10,000 speakers; data from Allison's 1979 phonology typescript plus Pallesen's 372-word list and text), listed among the six SLU languages with completed phonemic analysis (YK, NS.4, WS.1, CS.2, JM, SS.4). The catalog name 'Sibutu Sama' corresponds to this variety; Glottolog sout2918 'Southern Sama' also covers the Simunul (SS.2), Tandu-Bas (SS.1), Pahut (SS.3) and Sampulnaq (SS.5) varieties.

sources.quote: 'Stress in Southern Sinama is predictable. Lexical stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, and phrasal stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the phrase. The stress is retained by this syllable regardless of any reduplication or inflectional, or derivational affixing. Because of its predictable nature, the stress in the language is non-phonemic.' Examples 2-5 syllables all penultimate (e.g. [ka.si.ja.'li:.han]); syllabic nasals can bear stress (['m.boʔ]). Exception: 'the numbers presented below are stressed on the ultimate syllable': dikow' 'one', duwampu' 'twenty'
sources.note: Only recent primary description of Southern Sinama phonology (Simunul variety); confirms penultimate primary stress and adds a closed class of final-stressed numerals (dikow', -pu' decades) not mentioned by Allison 1979 for Sibutu — worth a caution line on the record.
